entries.title: Colophon
entries.summary: How this site is made.
entries.search:
How this site is made.

Writing. Everything starts as Markdown in Obsidian, in a vault that syncs over iCloud between laptop and phone. A note goes public when its visibility property says so; everything else stays in the vault.

Build. A Python 3.9 exporter (~1,700 lines; PyYAML, Pillow) reads the vault, keeps only public notes, strips location data from photos, and hands the result to Quartz v5, a TypeScript static-site generator running on Node 26 (unified, remark, rehype). Links to notes that aren't public yet stay as plain text until they are.

Interface. The stream, library, and training pages are ~2,000 lines of plain JavaScript and ~850 lines of CSS — no framework, no chart library. Every chart is hand-written SVG. Type is set in Geist and Geist Mono.

Training data. A Python importer talks to COROS over its official MCP interface (OAuth), pulls workouts, lap splits, and wellness data, and parses original FIT files with fitdecode for the second-by-second charts. Routes and coordinates never leave the laptop. Units are converted to miles and feet at the last moment, because the watch thinks in kilometres.

Publishing. A macOS LaunchAgent (a few lines of bash) syncs and rebuilds every three hours; commits go to GitHub, and GitHub Actions deploys to GitHub Pages. A small local app, the publishing desk, shows what's ready, what changed, and what needs attention.

Tests. 43 Python unit tests, mostly about not publishing things that shouldn't be published.

Credits. Built on Quartz (MIT). The linked-intro homepage, library, season strip, and daily log borrow ideas from Aaron Pham's garden. Colours: aubergine 120a1c, ivory ece6f1, orange ff9a3c.

entries.title: De-individualization through deskilling
entries.summary: Technology can drain the meaning out of work by quietly moving where understanding lives. It used to live in the mechanical: in the hands, in the senses, in the feel of something pushing back. Now it lives in computerized control. Our own i
entries.search:
Technology can drain the meaning out of work by quietly moving where understanding lives. It used to live in the mechanical: in the hands, in the senses, in the feel of something pushing back. Now it lives in computerized control. Our own interpretive muscles weaken while the software does the interpreting. Nobody decides this. Each handoff is a small, sensible convenience. Added up, you become the person who presses the button.

What’s special about working with the thing itself is that it argues back. Wood splits along the grain you missed. A sentence lands incorrectly and fails to convey your meaning. A patient’s story doesn’t exactly match the chart. That kind of contact with reality demands dialogue and through it you play a game with reality. Run it through black boxes of statistics and software and the dialogue stops. You get an answer instead of an encounter. The output improves, and the person producing it matters less: individual skill, and the identity built around it, is traded for better average performance across everyone using the software. It’s a good trade for the system. It’s a strange one for the individual, who ends up with a résumé of results and a shrinking inventory of individual abilities.

Take music. A century ago, if you wanted music in the house, someone in the house had to make it. The parlor piano was furniture and credential at once, proof of some intimacy with the thing. Then came the radio and the record player, and the piano became a place to put photographs. Playing was replaced by a needle scrolling over the skill of another. Music got better and more plentiful; musicianship got rarer. We gained Wagner and lost the uncle who could could somehow get through three of his songs.

The pattern generalizes. We’ve inherited conceptual and physical tools we can no longer make. Leonard Read pointed out that no single person knows how to make a pencil. Thomas Thwaites spent months building a toaster from scratch, ore and all, and got something that worked briefly before it melted. We assemble results we trust but can’t personally reproduce. Civilization is, in a sense, a giant agreement not to ask how anything works. Mostly that’s fine; it’s why we aren’t all subsistence farmers. The real question is which kinds of ignorance cost nothing and which ones cost something we wanted to keep.

Large language models blur the line between information and skill more than any technology I've used before it. Information could be looked up and a skill had to be grown by ingesting that information. An encyclopedia could tell you what a sonnet is but couldn’t write one. A model can, and it can insidiously make you feel like you wrote it while also sucking all the creativity out of it. It generates on the fly from pretrained weights, the crystallized knowledge of the past brought back to life to do something that looks a lot like fluid thinking. And unlike earlier black boxes, this one talks back. It will clarify, object and revise, which is everything I said gave real contact its meaning. But the conversation is with a summary of everyone, not with the thing itself. It argues back, but on behalf of the average.

Medicine is where this stops being an aesthetic complaint. AI may reduce the accuracy of any one diagnostician. In one 2025 study, endoscopists who had grown used to AI assistance found fewer precancerous polyps once it was switched off. The muscle weakened exactly as predicted. And yet the digital centaur, clinician and model reading together, still leads to better diagnoses overall. (The term comes from Kasparov’s human-plus-computer chess after Deep Blue.) For the patient, that’s the number that matters. I wouldn’t trade a missed tumor for a radiologist’s sense of self.

But the centaur has a structural weakness. It only beats the machine alone while the human half can still see something the machine can’t. Deskill the human enough and you don’t have a centaur; you have a horse with a passenger. So the question isn’t whether to use the tools. I will, gladly. It’s which muscles I keep exercising on purpose, knowing the tool would be faster. The parlor piano didn’t disappear because recordings were bad. It disappeared because nobody had a reason to practice, and the practicing was the point.

entries.title: Behave
entries.creator: Robert Sapolsky
entries.summary: Learned about changes in hormonal expression.
entries.search:
Learned about changes in hormonal expression.

Sapolsky's method is the useful part. Take one behavior and walk backward in time: the neurons that fired a second before, the hormones of the minutes and hours before, the environment of the preceding days, then adolescence, childhood, the womb, genes, culture, and finally evolution. Each chapter widens the lens by one step, and no single level gets to be the cause.

Hormones sit in the middle of that ladder, which makes them a good entry point. Sapolsky's recurring correction is that they rarely cause behavior outright; testosterone, for instance, tends to amplify tendencies already present rather than create new ones. It's the most patient possible answer to Nature vs Nurture, and it lands close to Nature Via Nurture — genes and environment as one tangled causal chain rather than rival teams. The Blank Slate argues the same from the other direction.

entries.title: Give the morning's best hours to deep work
entries.summary: Set up the morning to use its 3–4 hours of concentration, and let the rest of the day be carried by the wind and the remaining tasks.
entries.search:
Set up the morning to use its 3–4 hours of concentration, and let the rest of the day be carried by the wind and the remaining tasks.

Much better than cramming work that needs serious focus into short gaps where I can't focus deeply on it anyway. See Deep Work on attention residue.

It's scheduling by quality instead of quantity. An hour of real concentration does more than three hours of fragments, and fragments are what an unplanned afternoon tends to produce. Protecting the morning also takes a decision off the table — no weighing what to do first when the first thing is already decided (Decision quality falls as decision count rises).

The rest of the day can then be shallow without guilt, because the important work already happened. The failure mode is spending those hours on email and calling it a head start, which is the warning in Either you run the day or the day runs you. A walk between blocks is the cheapest reset on offer (The Cognitive Benefits of Interacting with Nature).

entries.title: A relentless focus on quality beats speed
entries.summary: I've been reaching for quick, easier solutions in the name of progress and efficiency — partly because I feel the need to finish faster and be more productive.
entries.search:
I've been reaching for quick, easier solutions in the name of progress and efficiency — partly because I feel the need to finish faster and be more productive.

With a relentless focus on quality, I make fewer mistakes, which limits the extra work I have to do in the first place, and the work itself is higher quality and higher impact. The interesting projects in front of me need the time and energy, plus that focus on quality, to develop the expertise they call for.

entries.title: Brains built for tribes are mismatched with modern technology
entries.summary: There's a significant problem in how our brains — shaped first for Paleolithic life, then for Neolithic life in small tribes, and later for organizing around cultural myths into larger social structures — interact with the technology we're
entries.search:
There's a significant problem in how our brains — shaped first for Paleolithic life, then for Neolithic life in small tribes, and later for organizing around cultural myths into larger social structures — interact with the technology we're exposed to now.

The modes of thinking cultivated by those older ways of living collide with modern tech, causing tension, conflict, and misaligned aims and incentives.

entries.title: Complaints reveal which needs are met
entries.summary: Humans are always going to complain — it's in our nature to acclimate to whatever condition we're in. So the complaints we have about our environment reflect how well our needs are already met.
entries.search:
Humans are always going to complain — it's in our nature to acclimate to whatever condition we're in. So the complaints we have about our environment reflect how well our needs are already met.

From Maslow's The Farther Reaches of Human Nature: low grumbles are about food, safety, belonging. Metagrumbles are about knowledge, beauty, creativity — metaneeds that only become available to complain about once the lower ones are handled. Someone complaining that the rose gardens in the park aren't cared for well enough is, in its way, a wonderful thing: it shows the height of life they're living at.

What a way to read a person's development — by the quality of their grumbling. The question becomes what they're complaining about: their ability to be actualized? The kinds of problems they're working on?

entries.title: Cardiometabolic risk factor analysis
entries.summary: A paper idea from early 2024, set as a six-month goal: how cardiometabolic risk factors cluster, and the role sleep plays. Got as far as a framework.
entries.search:
A paper idea from early 2024, set as a six-month goal: how cardiometabolic risk factors cluster, and the role sleep plays. Got as far as a framework.

Methods I was learning for it:

- Principal Component Analysis and factor analysis — collapse many correlated risk factors into a few underlying ones.
- An Intuitive Introduction to Multinomial Logit — the plan was to compare multinomial logit with factor analysis for cardiovascular risk assessment.

Anchor paper: Tsai et al. (2020), Factor analysis for the clustering of cardiometabolic risk factors and sedentary behavior. Five factors — adiposity, lipids, blood pressure, glucose, sedentary behavior — explained 69.4% of the variance; hsCRP clustered with adiposity, not with the other cardiometabolic factors.

Part of a larger goal that year to learn machine learning and write a paper by year's end.

entries.title: The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes
entries.summary: Really enjoyed it — political intrigue, character development, intertwined plot elements, and a fair amount of world-building drawn from the earlier films. The pacing was good, though I didn't expect a third act beyond his time as a mentor
entries.search:
Really enjoyed it — political intrigue, character development, intertwined plot elements, and a fair amount of world-building drawn from the earlier films. The pacing was good, though I didn't expect a third act beyond his time as a mentor and the Games themselves.

The prequel's question is how Coriolanus Snow, the future tyrant of the series, became one. The tenth Hunger Games are losing their audience, Capitol students are assigned as mentors to make the spectacle watchable, and Snow draws District 12's Lucy Gray Baird. The film follows a young man choosing control over the people he says he loves.

Running underneath is an argument about human nature: the Head Gamemaker, Dr. Gaul, holds that people without order turn on each other, which is the whole justification for the Games. That's the debate The Blank Slate picks apart, and the craft of steering people through their weaknesses is the subject of Weakness and manipulation in The Bonds of Interest. The Games themselves are a collective myth with a body count.

entries.title: Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
entries.creator: Serrano.Academy
entries.summary: Luis Serrano's channel explains machine learning with pictures before equations, and PCA suits the approach: a cloud of points, the direction along which they spread out most, then the next direction at right angles to it, and so on. Keep t
entries.search:
Luis Serrano's channel explains machine learning with pictures before equations, and PCA suits the approach: a cloud of points, the direction along which they spread out most, then the next direction at right angles to it, and so on. Keep the first few directions, drop the rest, and most of the variance survives in far fewer dimensions.

The cost is interpretability — the new axes are blends of the original variables, and naming them is an act of judgment (The Map is Not the Territory). The working notes are in Principal Component Analysis; the reason for learning it was Cardiometabolic risk factor analysis, where a dozen correlated risk factors are begging to be summarized.

entries.title: Principal component analysis
entries.summary: A dimensionality-reduction method: re-express many variables as a smaller set of uncorrelated linear combinations of them.
entries.search:
A dimensionality-reduction method: re-express many variables as a smaller set of uncorrelated linear combinations of them.

The steps:
- Fit a line of best fit through the data. The vector along it is an eigenvector; the proportions of each variable in it are the loading scores.
- The eigenvectors and eigenvalues come from the covariance matrix — variances on the diagonal, covariances off it.
- An eigenvalue is the variance captured by that component. All eigenvalues sum to the total variance of the original variables, so each one's share is the percentage of variation it explains.
- Project the data onto the eigenvectors with the largest eigenvalues. A scree plot shows the variation per component; a common cutoff is eigenvalue  1.

Things to remember:
- You can have as many components as original variables.
- PCA does nothing if the original variables aren't correlated.
- Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin tests whether variables are factorable: overall  0.5, individual  0.8.

entries.title: The map is not the territory
entries.summary: A map of reality isn't reality — maps are imperfect.
entries.search:
A map of reality isn't reality — maps are imperfect.

We need abstractions: descriptions, theories, models. But every map has three problems:
- It can be incorrect without our realizing it.
- It's a reduction of the real thing, so it loses fidelity.
- It needs interpretation, which can introduce major errors.

The phrase is Alfred Korzybski's, and its usefulness lies in how often it's forgotten. A diagnosis is a map of a patient, a model a map of data, a self-image a map of a person, and each one quietly becomes the thing it describes if nobody checks it against the ground.

The fix isn't to stop making maps — reasoning without them is impossible — but to remember which is which and to update when the ground disagrees. The Voice Inside Your Head is a map-maker that never stops drawing; Emic and etic is about whose map you're using; Principal Component Analysis is a deliberately lossy one, chosen for what it leaves out.

entries.title: Group selection vs individual selection
entries.summary: Groups are a collection of individuals each acting to optimize their own well-being. That includes supposed altruism — we're altruistic when there's a benefit likely to pay off over time.
entries.search:
Groups are a collection of individuals each acting to optimize their own well-being. That includes supposed altruism — we're altruistic when there's a benefit likely to pay off over time.

Assuming a group will be inherently altruistic ignores drift and mutation. In the real world a selfish mutant would be advantaged and spread, exploiting everyone else's altruism.

- Signaling theory. Even acts with no possible payback signal to the community who is trustworthy and generous.
- Tit for tat. Further reading: The Selfish Gene.

entries.title: Limbic friction
entries.summary: The resistance you feel when you know there's something you can do and you're refusing to do it — the friction my brain generates whenever I want to start an activity.
entries.search:
The resistance you feel when you know there's something you can do and you're refusing to do it — the friction my brain generates whenever I want to start an activity.

One way through it: make a list of painful activities and make yourself do them. Steepen and deepen the trough of amotivation and pain:
- cold shower or ice bath
- a meditation session
- a set number of pushups, squats, situps
- learning something difficult

entries.title: Productivity means intentional progress, not busyness
entries.summary: Productivity should only be defined by how far the desired activity got accomplished. It's tied to an intentional goal, or the intentional process of completing something — it doesn't mean busy.
entries.search:
Productivity should only be defined by how far the desired activity got accomplished. It's tied to an intentional goal, or the intentional process of completing something — it doesn't mean busy.

As long as I'm acting intentionally toward my goals, that's productive. Whatever pulls me away from what I want to accomplish is distraction. Written while reading Psycho-Cybernetics: pick something to aim the goal-seeking mechanism at — finishing work, the gym, reading, being present with people.

entries.title: Self-referential thoughts should earn their keep
entries.summary: Every self-referential thought should go under the magnifying glass: is it contributing to action toward my goals?
entries.search:
Every self-referential thought should go under the magnifying glass: is it contributing to action toward my goals?

What good does thinking I'm unintelligent do? It makes me shirk and stop taking in information, believing I can't understand it.

The test is functional, not moral. "I'm bad at this" isn't wrong because it's negative; it's wrong because it does no work — it doesn't change the next action except to make it less likely. "I don't understand this yet, so I need an example" is just as self-referential, and it earns its place.

The stakes are higher than mood: "We can become, neurologically, what we think." — Nicholas Carr, The Shallows Repeated thoughts are rehearsal. The audit is the same move cognitive therapy borrowed from the Stoics (Disturbed not by things but by our view of them); the thing under audit is The Voice Inside Your Head.

entries.title: When I feel purposeless or anxious, I should work out
entries.summary: After vigorous cardio I feel much more comfortable in my own mind — not racing, grounded and stable.
entries.search:
After vigorous cardio I feel much more comfortable in my own mind — not racing, grounded and stable.

The axiom to remember: whenever I feel depressed, purposeless, or anxious, work out. Run, walk, get the heart rate up, bring the body to physical exhaustion. Once I'm no longer brimming with energy for the myriad ideas my mind throws at me, I can be selective and pick the ones worth pursuing.

entries.title: People pay far less attention to you than you think
entries.summary: People really don't care what you're doing nearly as much as you think. They're paying attention to their own lives, their own realities, what's going on with them.
entries.search:
People really don't care what you're doing nearly as much as you think. They're paying attention to their own lives, their own realities, what's going on with them.

Sitting and observing a conversation without a goal: the words matter less than you'd think. Tonality carries much of the meaning in human conversation.

Psychologists call it the spotlight effect. In the classic study, students sent into a room wearing an embarrassing T-shirt guessed that about half the people there noticed; the actual figure was closer to a quarter. Everyone else is busy being the main character of their own day.

The self is loud mostly to itself: "Had the human self been installed with a mute button or off switch, the self would not be the curse to happiness that it often is." — Mark Leary, quoted in Golden The useful conclusion isn't that nobody cares, but that trying something and looking foolish costs far less than it feels. See Self-referential thoughts should earn their keep and Present Orientation on getting out of the self-conscious loop.

entries.title: Four social theories of global health
entries.summary: From a medical anthropology class in Seville. Medical anthropology studies health, healing, and illness within their political, economic, and social context.
entries.search:
From a medical anthropology class in Seville. Medical anthropology studies health, healing, and illness within their political, economic, and social context.

1. Unintended consequences of social action. Institutions trying to do good cause later harm. Forced vaccination campaigns bred vaccine hesitancy that undermined later public-health efforts.
2. Social suffering.
   - Health systems can do harm — medical error, waiting times, misdiagnosis, poorly informed treatment.
   - Social causes produce health problems — poverty, high-stress environments, food deserts, no sanitation or clean water, toxic exposure.
   - Social and health problems are hard to separate: is someone ill because of a disease, or the chronic stress of living in poverty? Social policy and health policy are often one and the same.
   - The individual isn't the only sufferer. A person with Alzheimer's has a family watching them lose their memory; disease ripples through social networks.
3. Social construction of reality. What health is, what counts as acceptable treatment and healthy behavior — all depend on the cultural reality people live in.
4. Biopower. Governments and corporations shape how our biology manifests — which products they offer, which choices they allow, which body types get manufactured consent.

entries.title: Grades and competition crowd out intrinsic motivation
entries.summary: Competition and grading are external motivators, and they reduce the drive that's intrinsic. When an early sense of security, autonomy, social support, and ability is threatened and made contingent on external rewards, a person has to work
entries.search:
Competition and grading are external motivators, and they reduce the drive that's intrinsic. When an early sense of security, autonomy, social support, and ability is threatened and made contingent on external rewards, a person has to work against their intrinsically motivating forces.

My ideal state is being entirely intrinsically motivated, while still having the markers of success in the society we live in.

Someone had to design the learning systems we're put through; they don't arise naturally. Would I have been taught how to naturally retain and remember, or would it always have been a struggle? And in my own classes I find it frankly ridiculous that we're told to learn in these ways instead of by ourselves — online, or reading to learn.

entries.title: Decision quality falls as decision count rises
entries.summary: The quality of my decisions deteriorates as I make more of them over a day. Decision fatigue looks like inaction, decision avoidance, procrastination, short-sighted and erratic behavior.
entries.search:
The quality of my decisions deteriorates as I make more of them over a day. Decision fatigue looks like inaction, decision avoidance, procrastination, short-sighted and erratic behavior.

So the way to make good decisions is to make fewer of them. Systematize or eliminate most of the daily ones — how I wake up, what I do in the morning, how I work out, what I eat. Remove the rational mind's ability to negotiate. Let cues and triggers do the deciding (the house lights turn red at a set time).

Same idea in The Organized Mind: the brain's decision-making network can't prioritize which decisions deserve its attention. Every decision taxes it, so restricting how many I face conserves it.

The other way to spend less on a decision: Constraint relaxation.

entries.title: Reading without review mostly evaporates
entries.summary: There's no purpose to reading educational material without making review material for it. Otherwise I won't make progress in my understanding.
entries.search:
There's no purpose to reading educational material without making review material for it. Otherwise I won't make progress in my understanding.

My retention of a text depends on how long it's been since I last read it and how many days in a row I read and reviewed it — spaced repetition and consistency, plainly. Writing and speaking about what I learned, then reviewing and speaking about it again, would help too.

What the review material should look like:
1. Cards I can review in a year and still know what source they came from and what concept they mean.
2. Atomic — the smallest possible unit. The organization comes from integrating those atoms into my own schema.

Two years later in medical school, same lesson from Anki: information under regular spaced repetition is closer at hand than anything recalled after long gaps.

entries.title: The words I know limit the thoughts I can think
entries.summary: Learning Spanish: it's hard to transfer how I think into the language. Thoughts flow differently, bounded by the words I know. I think less politically and less complexly, because the words don't come quickly. In English I can convey though
entries.search:
Learning Spanish: it's hard to transfer how I think into the language. Thoughts flow differently, bounded by the words I know. I think less politically and less complexly, because the words don't come quickly. In English I can convey thoughts with subtlety — or, put another way, be wordy. In Spanish there's no room for long, drawn-out sentences; I have to finish forming the thought first.

The other direction is true too: people who know different languages live a different experience of the world. Different words for facets of nature and environment make reality richer and more detailed.

And words have a cost. They might reduce our capacity to experience the world directly — pulling us outside the body, sorting things into categories. What I can experience in any state of mind isn't fully expressible in words; it's the difference between labeling an experience and not labeling it.

On learning vocabulary: mapping a Spanish word back to English is three layers of processing (thing → English → Spanish) instead of two. Better to tie the word directly to an image, idea, or felt sensation.

entries.title: The Bonds of Interest
entries.creator: Jacinto Benavente
entries.summary: Read for a Nobel Prizes in Literature class. My essay: Weakness and manipulation in The Bonds of Interest.
entries.search:
Read for a Nobel Prizes in Literature class. My essay: Weakness and manipulation in The Bonds of Interest.

Jacinto Benavente's 1907 comedy borrows its masks from the commedia dell'arte: two penniless adventurers, the romantic Leandro and his scheming servant Crispín, arrive in a city and con their way into society by pretending to be rich. Crispín pulls every string — he works out what each person wants and sells it back to them. Benavente won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1922.

The dry joke is in the title: everyone is held together by interest, and love wins only once the debts are settled. See Weakness and manipulation in The Bonds of Interest for the close reading, and Can literature be judged like chemistry for the class's larger question about prizes and merit.

entries.title: Emic and etic
entries.summary: Two perspectives on a culture, named after phonetic vs phonemic:
entries.search:
Two perspectives on a culture, named after phonetic vs phonemic:

- Etic (from phonetic — the sounds) — the outsider's objective evaluation of a culture's activities or customs.
- Emic (from phonemic — the meaning) — the insider's perspective on what those activities and conditions mean.

A related point from the same class: we all have the capacity for the same primary emotions across cultures, but how they're interpreted and understood depends on the cultural context we live in.

entries.title: Rapt: Attention and the Focused Life
entries.creator: Winifred Gallagher
entries.summary: Personally, I found it quite great. It covered a lot of themes I'd already read, and a few sweeping cultural claims don't hold up — but there's much truth in it. It doesn't claim meditation is the answer; it argues that attention lies at th
entries.search:
Personally, I found it quite great. It covered a lot of themes I'd already read, and a few sweeping cultural claims don't hold up — but there's much truth in it. It doesn't claim meditation is the answer; it argues that attention lies at the core of our existence.

The most interesting part: research on flow, and how early-childhood experiences set up the capacity for difficult work that makes later concentration and flow possible. Analyzing that across cultures could be fruitful.

A possible meditation target: two spheres of attention, top-down and bottom-up. We can set our objects of awareness — whether we attend to the positive or the negative is up to us.

entries.title: Positive and negative life experiences
entries.summary: Positive life experiences cluster in young adulthood (20–45), with the adoption of more social roles — living alone, a job, new friends, partners, other responsibilities. Over that period, neuroticism goes down.
entries.search:
Positive life experiences cluster in young adulthood (20–45), with the adoption of more social roles — living alone, a job, new friends, partners, other responsibilities. Over that period, neuroticism goes down.

How are we defining a positive life experience, though, and why would taking on more roles reduce neuroticism? Is autonomy the driving factor in the growth of the individual? What else could explain it?

Negative life experiences are spread more evenly across the lifespan — they're deviations from life's normal progress — though they still trend upward over time.

entries.title: Name overwhelm early or it becomes burnout
entries.summary: Being able to identify the feeling of being overwhelmed is crucial to managing workload. Failing to notice it is a recipe for burnout.
entries.search:
Being able to identify the feeling of being overwhelmed is crucial to managing workload. Failing to notice it is a recipe for burnout.

Overwhelm is a signal with a short shelf life. Named early, it's a scheduling problem: too many commitments, some of which can be dropped, delegated, or moved. Ignored, it compounds into exhaustion and cynicism, and by then the problem is no longer the calendar.

The naming is the hard part, because busyness feels like competence from the inside (Productivity means intentional progress, not busyness). A journal helps by making the pattern visible before it becomes a crisis (What journaling is for), and the structural fix is protecting a few hours for what matters and letting the rest wait (Give the morning's best hours to deep work).

entries.title: Sapiens
entries.creator: Yuval Noah Harari
entries.summary:
- Homo sapiens came out on top of competition with other human species, though I don't think the book really analyzes why sapiens were more adept.
- What distinguishes humans: forming social groups oriented toward goals, using myth and cult
entries.search:
- Homo sapiens came out on top of competition with other human species, though I don't think the book really analyzes why sapiens were more adept.
- What distinguishes humans: forming social groups oriented toward goals, using myth and culture to organize. Groups built on intimate bonds top out around 150 people. Beyond that, cultural myths, laws, rules, religion, and gods — structures that exist only in other people's minds — coordinate effort. See Collective myths.
- Fire: light, and cooked food that cut the time and energy spent on digestion, supposedly freeing energy for a much larger brain. Interestingly, Neanderthals had bigger crania than we do.
- Some of Harari's arguments aren't entirely believable; others give a lot of food for thought.

Finishing it, I realized I need a more single-minded approach to taking in information. There's no doing two things at once, paying attention to two things at once.

entries.title: Collective myths
entries.summary: An idea I kept running into across my reading: collective myths bond us together and form the basis for our social hierarchies — what we believe in, pursue, look up to; what we take as good and bad, right and wrong, valuable and not. They s
entries.search:
An idea I kept running into across my reading: collective myths bond us together and form the basis for our social hierarchies — what we believe in, pursue, look up to; what we take as good and bad, right and wrong, valuable and not. They shape how we think and try to understand the world.

They let us feel connected to and understanding of the people around us, and they give us the organizational structure and shared vision for larger projects.

Take the American Dream: rugged individualism, Puritan hard work, inalienable rights, the idea that a man should govern himself rather than be beholden to a larger body — voicing his opinion when larger projects need it, keeping his own sphere of influence with limited government.

From Sapiens: humans top out at about 150 people for structures built on intimate bonds. Past that, cultural myths, laws, religion, gods — structures that exist only in other people's minds — coordinate effort toward shared goals. And The Search for Meaning: we don't escape myth by sticking to "facts"; understanding anything means encoding it through mythic techniques.

entries.title: Motivation follows action
entries.summary: I wait for motivation to exercise, and it doesn't come. I know the answer: motivation follows action. I'm just not taking any action.
entries.search:
I wait for motivation to exercise, and it doesn't come. I know the answer: motivation follows action. I'm just not taking any action.

Russell says something similar about the feeling that everything is vanity — those moods can't be changed by rational argument or words, only by the necessity of action. See The Conquest of Happiness.

Russell's version is less about mood than about design: the human animal is built for some struggle, and "the mere absence of effort from his life removes an essential ingredient of happiness." — Bertrand Russell, The Conquest of Happiness Waiting for motivation is a way of removing the effort and expecting the happiness anyway.

The mechanism isn't mysterious. Starting produces small signals of progress, and progress is what motivation feeds on; waiting produces nothing. The trick is making the first step small enough to be beneath negotiation — shoes on, one set, one page. Limbic friction names the resistance at the threshold; When I feel purposeless or anxious, I should work out is the applied version.

entries.title: What I attend to becomes my life
entries.summary: Life is attention. What we pay attention to sets the direction of our lives and defines our lived experience of them.
entries.search:
Life is attention. What we pay attention to sets the direction of our lives and defines our lived experience of them.

To focus deeper, block out irrelevant stimuli and train attention to stay rooted on its object — meditation in its forms (loving-kindness, open monitoring, focused attention) is the scientifically supported way.

The mind will focus on what it desires, but I'm a function of the awareness of the mind; I can choose the salient cues and hone in on them. I keep forgetting I'm responsible for my mental state: I can move attention toward what fulfills me, which is usually in the outside world. Caught up in thought, I keep feeding the same emotional cycle.

Think of the brain as an engine and consciousness as the steering wheel: wherever you direct attention, the brain follows. The trouble starts when you steer toward an unsolvable problem. (From Hyperfocus.)

entries.title: Hurry leaves no room for depth
entries.summary: I hurry through life. I want things done fast, I want "better" ways of doing things — and I often can't find the patience and calm to hear a friend out, which is the truest display of empathy.
entries.search:
I hurry through life. I want things done fast, I want "better" ways of doing things — and I often can't find the patience and calm to hear a friend out, which is the truest display of empathy.

What's the belief underneath? Anything that wants the world to unfold in a way it doesn't. Hurry, at the core. There's no room for reflection during hurry. No room for kindness. No room for deep thought — hurry is the antithesis of deep. We can't keep a sense of calm and patience and understanding while constantly in the throes of hurry.

entries.title: Deep Work
entries.creator: Cal Newport
entries.summary:
- Great Restructuring — disruptive technology lowers the value of an individual's labor; employers will increasingly hire machines over people. Further reading: Tyler Cowen's Average Is Over.
- Attention residue — after switching tasks, wor
entries.search:
- Great Restructuring — disruptive technology lowers the value of an individual's labor; employers will increasingly hire machines over people. Further reading: Tyler Cowen's Average Is Over.
- Attention residue — after switching tasks, working memory and attention stay partly on the last one, and performance on the new one drops.
- Distracted high performers — few decision-making roles don't need the quiet of deep work. CEOs are paid for their judgment on solutions, not for producing them.

Newport's core claim is economic before it's personal: "the ability to perform deep work is becoming increasingly rare at exactly the same time it is becoming increasingly valuable in our economy." — Cal Newport, Deep Work The Great Restructuring is the demand side of that sentence. Attention residue is the supply-side problem: every quick check of email leaves part of the mind behind, so a day of short switches is a day of half-attention.

The practical version lives in Give the morning's best hours to deep work; the temperamental version in Hurry leaves no room for depth. The Shallows makes the same case from the neuroscience side, and Decision quality falls as decision count rises explains why Newport leans on rituals — fixed times, fixed places — to do so much of the work: they remove the decision to start.

entries.title: Shared presence is enough for friendship
entries.summary: Social interactions don't need to signal complete understanding, reach a shared understanding of a topic, or even touch our baseline emotions. They can be as simple as shared presence — someone in the room, a repeated interaction, a warm wa
entries.search:
Social interactions don't need to signal complete understanding, reach a shared understanding of a topic, or even touch our baseline emotions. They can be as simple as shared presence — someone in the room, a repeated interaction, a warm wave from a regular you see.

Those are the interactions that activate the prosocial networks of the brain and the positive response that comes with them. In what way am I failing to take advantage of them?

entries.title: Group conversation reverts to the mean
entries.summary: An individual is a crowd, and a crowd is an individual. That's how talking with groups feels: the reversion to the mean. The conversation can't escape or change topic except to jump to the most identifiable idea, rather than the deepest tho
entries.search:
An individual is a crowd, and a crowd is an individual. That's how talking with groups feels: the reversion to the mean. The conversation can't escape or change topic except to jump to the most identifiable idea, rather than the deepest thought or insight we could try to inspire in each other.

Part of it is arithmetic. In a group, every topic has to be accessible to everyone present, so the conversation drifts to the intersection of interests, and the intersection is small. Part of it is social risk: a strange idea said to one person is a conversation; said to six, it's a performance.

Depth needs a small audience and some tolerance for silence, which is why one-on-one goes further — and why Shared presence is enough for friendship: the group's job may be presence rather than insight. The shared reference points a group falls back on are Collective myths in miniature, and People pay far less attention to you than you think is the reminder that the performance risk is smaller than it feels.

entries.title: Clear writing comes from clear thinking
entries.summary: Reading back my own writing, I fail to be concise and add filler. Even some of the "ands" are just a wish to be verbose. State what I feel, without adding justifications and reasons for it.
entries.search:
Reading back my own writing, I fail to be concise and add filler. Even some of the "ands" are just a wish to be verbose. State what I feel, without adding justifications and reasons for it.

To what extent have I prioritized complex sentences over clear ideas? Cut the unnecessary, verbose phrasing into authoritative, direct statements. Hard-to-read writing frustrates readers; it's only accessible to people who already believe you have something to say, never to someone coming to your words for the first time.

Clarity in writing comes from clarity in thought — the two are inextricably linked. Avoiding that work lands you in pseudo-intellectual territory: knowledge and phrases that carry depth only at first glance.

Being a writer isn't just having ideas; it's writing about them well — using the full extent of the language while minimizing complexity. Getting words onto the page is easy for me now. Going back over them and conveying them clearly still escapes me. (On Writing Well helped: much of what passes for grammar is really style.)

entries.title: Constraint relaxation
entries.summary: Some problems are effectively intractable — they're solved in O(n!) time, so the truly optimal answer can't be reached in a tractable amount of time. Relax the constraints and you reach a semi-optimal solution in a fraction of the time.
entries.search:
Some problems are effectively intractable — they're solved in O(n!) time, so the truly optimal answer can't be reached in a tractable amount of time. Relax the constraints and you reach a semi-optimal solution in a fraction of the time.

Its cousin is overfitting: certain data values get over-prioritized, and the model stops generalizing beyond the data set it was built on.

Both carry over to human decisions. I can overfit a decision — too many variables, too many what-ifs. Relaxing the constraints cuts through it. The question that does this: what job would you pick if you won the lottery? It lets me look past the variables that distract from the intention behind the choice, and decide with less effort and less excessive weighing of every factor.

entries.title: In the Name of Identity: Violence and the Need to Belong
entries.creator: Amin Maalouf
entries.summary: Three parts. First, what identity is: not any single affiliation or piece of heritage, but the combination of all of them that makes a person unique — it can't be divided into halves or thirds. Second, a history of modernization and religio
entries.search:
Three parts. First, what identity is: not any single affiliation or piece of heritage, but the combination of all of them that makes a person unique — it can't be divided into halves or thirds. Second, a history of modernization and religion's role as universal values of human dignity spread; examples of tolerance in both Christianity and Islam; and how tying modernity to the West made non-Western groups feel threatened and cling harder to one facet of identity. Third, how to unite people under modernity while keeping their identities.

Ideas I marked: everyone has a "vertical" heritage from ancestors and community and a "horizontal" one from their contemporaries; we assert our differences so fiercely precisely because we're less and less different; traditions deserve respect only insofar as they respect fundamental human rights.

A poem in class about indigenous people cast aside as irrelevant reminded me of this book: is there a way to keep traditional ways while lifting quality of life? What does progress even mean?

entries.title: The Shallows: What the Internet Is Doing to Our Brains
entries.creator: Nicholas Carr
entries.summary: Carr, after McLuhan: outside of the content a medium carries, the medium itself changes our patterns of perception — how we think as individuals and as a society.
entries.search:
Carr, after McLuhan: outside of the content a medium carries, the medium itself changes our patterns of perception — how we think as individuals and as a society.

- The internet lets us offload memory and think more interrelationally. That offloading probably comes at a cost: less ability to read and understand long-form, and more trouble remembering what we've handed off to silicon.
- Plasticity cuts both ways — Monkey Brain Mapping Experiment. "We can become, neurologically, what we think."
- Time-Keeping: for most of history, time was a continuous, cyclical flow. Things just took as long as they took; there wasn't a way to measure whether something was done "better."
- Progression of Language: the phonetic alphabet made an economy of characters. Deep reading needed a shift from bottom-up to top-down attention.
- The internet seizes attention only to scatter it. My read: what we lose is the ability to sit with one idea for a long time — shorter attention spans, shallower dives, bite-sized messages as the norm of communication and of understanding.
- Linear readers comprehend more, remember more, learn more than readers of hyperlinked text. Effects of Hyperlinks on Learning, Cognitive Load.
- When journals moved online, scholars cited fewer and more recent articles — the opposite of what you'd expect.
- Technological Determinists vs Instrumentalists.

entries.title: Darwin's idea
entries.summary: Natural selection: organisms vary, the variants that suit the needs of their environment are selected for, and the population changes.
entries.search:
Natural selection: organisms vary, the variants that suit the needs of their environment are selected for, and the population changes.

When Darwin proposed it, the unit of heredity — the gene — hadn't been identified. Mendel's work would come out years later and take much longer to reach mainstream science. Groundbreaking as the idea was, it took a lot of further work to show it was right and displace the paradigms of the time.

See Galapagos Finch, and the idea it displaced: Law of Use and Disuse.

entries.title: Galapagos finch
entries.summary: One of the observations that led Darwin to natural selection: 14 finch species on the Galapagos whose main difference was the beak, each one suited to how that species fed.
entries.search:
One of the observations that led Darwin to natural selection: 14 finch species on the Galapagos whose main difference was the beak, each one suited to how that species fed.

They share a single common ancestor, so the differences really are adaptations. Field work has since watched selection happen in these populations: in years of heavy rain or drought, different food sources become common, and the species (and individuals) that can reach them thrive.

The same work shows how the birds keep species apart — visual cues (beak, appearance) and song — which prevents cross-species breeding that would otherwise homogenize the gene pool.

entries.title: Law of use and disuse
entries.summary: Crystallized by Jean-Baptiste Lamarck: changes in an animal's morphology from use (or disuse) accumulate and lead to differences between species.
entries.search:
Crystallized by Jean-Baptiste Lamarck: changes in an animal's morphology from use (or disuse) accumulate and lead to differences between species.

Wrong, but significant — it questioned the permanence of species, whether they could change at all.

The textbook example is the giraffe: stretch toward high leaves, the neck lengthens a little, and the offspring inherit the stretch. Darwin's alternative needs no effort from the giraffe — variation already exists, and the longer-necked ones simply leave more descendants (Darwin's Idea, Galapagos Finch).

Heredity turned out messier than either picture: "like produces like," and "like does not always produce like." — Knopik et al., Behavioral Genetics Lamarck lost the argument on inheritance, but the idea keeps reappearing in softer forms — epigenetic marks, and the intuition behind most self-improvement that effort gets written into what you become. Within one lifetime that's roughly true; across a lineage it mostly isn't. Nature Via Nurture covers the nuance.

entries.title: Mendel's law of independent assortment
entries.summary: The law: inheriting one allele doesn't affect inheriting another.
entries.search:
The law: inheriting one allele doesn't affect inheriting another.

In reality, false. Alleles can be linked — having one makes you more likely to have the other — because of where they sit on the chromosome. Genes close together tend to stay together through recombination. The distance is measured in centimorgans.

That exception is useful: linkage helps locate genes. Once a gene's location is mapped, genetic testing becomes possible, and its protein product can be studied toward a therapeutic.

Two single-gene examples of Mendel's first law:
- Huntington disease — dominant; 50% of an affected parent's children inherit it. Starts in middle adulthood with personality changes, forgetfulness, involuntary movements; ends in loss of motor control and intellect.
- Phenylketonuria — recessive; the enzyme that processes phenylalanine doesn't work, causing cognitive deficits. Found when blood tests showed high phenylalanine in people with intellectual disability.

entries.title: Morbidity risk estimate
entries.summary: The chance of being affected by a disorder over an entire lifetime, age-corrected — because the risk of getting a disease often depends on age. Schizophrenia, for example, doesn't show until late adolescence or later.
entries.search:
The chance of being affected by a disorder over an entire lifetime, age-corrected — because the risk of getting a disease often depends on age. Schizophrenia, for example, doesn't show until late adolescence or later.

Schizophrenia lifetime risk by relation to someone affected: second-degree relative 4%, first-degree 9%, fraternal twin 17%, identical twin 48%.

The schizophrenia numbers are the textbook case for genetic influence: risk climbs with relatedness. Galton would have liked them — "nature prevails enormously over nurture" — Francis Galton, quoted in Behavioral Genetics — but they're also the textbook case for the limits. Identical twins share essentially all their genes, and the concordance still stops near half.

Whatever makes up the other half isn't in the sequence, which is Nature vs Nurture in two numbers; Nature Via Nurture explains why the two terms resist separation. The age correction matters for the same reason survival statistics do: without it, a nineteen-year-old who hasn't yet developed the disorder counts as unaffected, and the risk gets quietly understated. Source: Behavioral Genetics.

entries.title: Francis Galton
entries.summary: English polymath, another grandson of Erasmus Darwin, and the first to apply statistics to the inheritance of intelligence. No IQ tests existed yet, so he used other measures of competence — ability, and "reputation" for contributing to soc
entries.search:
English polymath, another grandson of Erasmus Darwin, and the first to apply statistics to the inheritance of intelligence. No IQ tests existed yet, so he used other measures of competence — ability, and "reputation" for contributing to society.

Came up with correlation, championed regression to the mean, and devised measures like the median and quartiles.

On Nature vs Nurture he concluded that nature prevails enormously. He wasn't the first to suggest a mechanism of heredity for behavior, but he was the first to document it extensively. He also originated eugenics — which fed ideas of racial purity (Fatal Invention).

entries.title: Nature vs nurture
entries.summary: Which contributes more to how an organism turns out — genes or environment?
entries.search:
Which contributes more to how an organism turns out — genes or environment?

Francis Galton decided nature "prevails enormously" over nurture, at least for extraordinary traits. Later discoveries disproved the strong version, but he was the one who backed a claim about heredity of behavior with research.

What I took from Nature Via Nurture:
- The paradox of heritability. The more we equalize opportunity in a society, the more the remaining variation in performance comes down to genes.
- Genes as agents of nurture. As people age, less of their intelligence correlates with shared environment and more with genes. Two kids in one home may perform alike early; once they choose their own environments, their genes steer them apart.
- Nurture can be as irreversible as nature — critical periods in vision and language show it.

To forcibly exist on either side of this argument would be a failure to understand the relationship. There's flexibility within the confines of the structure nature gave me. Part of my person is flexible and part isn't — part is amenable to argument, and part is enforcing behaviors passed down through inheritance.

entries.title: The Cognitive Benefits of Interacting with Nature
entries.creator: Berman, Jonides, Kaplan
entries.summary: 2008. The study behind my Attention Restoration Theory note.
entries.search:
2008. The study behind my Attention Restoration Theory note.

The design is simple enough to remember. Participants took a walk either in an arboretum or along busy city streets, then repeated a backward digit-span test; directed attention improved after the nature walk and not after the urban one. A second experiment found a similar benefit from simply viewing pictures of nature rather than urban scenes.

The explanation is Attention Restoration Theory: nature holds attention softly, letting the effortful, directed kind recover. The practical upshot is less glamorous than any productivity app — a walk between deep-work blocks (Give the morning's best hours to deep work) — and it puts a mechanism under What I attend to becomes my life.

entries.title: Attention Restoration Theory
entries.summary: An approach to restoring attention. Environments with stimuli that modestly engage involuntary attention let directed attention recover.
entries.search:
An approach to restoring attention. Environments with stimuli that modestly engage involuntary attention let directed attention recover.

Attention splits into bottom-up (involuntary) and top-down (voluntary). Directed attention is the part of top-down attention that has to suppress distracting stimulation — and it's the part that tires.

The study (The Cognitive Benefits of Interacting with Nature): people walked for an hour in either an urban or a natural setting. The nature walkers did better on the backward digit-span test and on an Attention Network Task, and their mood improved (though mood wasn't what explained the attention gains).

- Backward digit span — listen to sequences of 3–9 digits, repeat them backwards. Measures directed-attention performance.
- PANAS (Positive and Negative Affect Schedule) — rate mood adjectives 1–5 for how well they describe you right now.

I moved seats once just to stop looking at dirt — actively implementing this. I wonder whether it actually changes performance on attention tasks.

entries.title: Modality effect
entries.summary: How the mode of presenting material affects memory and learning.
entries.search:
How the mode of presenting material affects memory and learning.

For serial recall, auditory beats visual (4.8 vs 5.36 words).

This relationship is interesting. Words are first taken in as visual images and then translated into their language components, so it would follow that presenting language-based material by ear is more efficient. There might also be something in how information enters working memory — whether running two modalities at once uses cognitive resources more efficiently.

entries.title: Progression of language
entries.summary: The move from pictorial to phonetic alphabets changed our mental capacities.
entries.search:
The move from pictorial to phonetic alphabets changed our mental capacities.

Sumerian cuneiform and Egyptian hieroglyphs were logosyllabic: the reader first had to analyze a character to work out how it was being used. That took more processing, and made literacy slow to learn and slow to spread.

The Greeks' phonetic alphabet created an economy of characters — less time and attention to recognize symbols, fewer cognitive resources. Brain studies comparing readers of phonetic and pictorial scripts back this up.

The cost of abstraction: McLuhan thought preliterate people had a more "sensuous" involvement with the world. Literacy and the analytical thinking it brings let us abstract away from lived experience — and detach from feeling.

entries.title: Split-attention effect
entries.summary: Extraneous cognitive load caused by how information is presented and organized. The classic case: a geometry diagram with the information you need to solve for its sides and angles printed separately, so you keep looking back and forth betw
entries.search:
Extraneous cognitive load caused by how information is presented and organized. The classic case: a geometry diagram with the information you need to solve for its sides and angles printed separately, so you keep looking back and forth between the two.

The fix is boring and effective: put the labels on the diagram, integrate text and figure, make the eye travel less. Holding one source in mind while searching the other is pure overhead — working memory spent on the layout instead of the geometry (Cognitive Load).

The other workaround is to move part of the information into a different channel — narrate the text while the eyes stay on the figure — which is the Modality Effect. Hyperlinks are the same problem at web scale (Effects of Hyperlinks on Learning), and so is any textbook that puts the figure on the next page.

entries.title: The voice inside your head
entries.summary: The voice in our head is constantly trying to find a comfortable resting place — internal coherence, the brain's need to fit new information into its existing schemas. It will change viewpoints and shift perspective to get there. It reminds
entries.search:
The voice in our head is constantly trying to find a comfortable resting place — internal coherence, the brain's need to fit new information into its existing schemas. It will change viewpoints and shift perspective to get there. It reminds me of the hedonic treadmill: this voice keeps moving the set-point for silence.

Is the voice me? No — I'm the one observing it. Put three objects in front of you and ask which one you are; none of them, you're the one looking. Same for the inner voice.

The commotion the mind makes about life is the real problem. Thinking about how things should change, or disliking how they are, does nothing to change them.

Why do we narrate? Labeling what we observe makes us feel we have a relationship with it — it's been seen, labeled, judged, run through our values and history. There's always some thought that makes the experience feel controlled: noticing it's cold, then comforting yourself that you'll be home in a few minutes. What about that thought was necessary?

entries.title: Time-keeping
entries.summary: The clock made "the abstract framework of divided time" the point of reference for thought and action — and with it, belief in a world of mathematically measurable sequences.
entries.search:
The clock made "the abstract framework of divided time" the point of reference for thought and action — and with it, belief in a world of mathematically measurable sequences.

- For most of history, time was a continuous, cyclical flow, set by agrarian rhythms. Things just took as long as they took; there was no way to measure whether something was done "better."
- Personal timekeeping put every individual in control of their own time — possibly a stimulus to Western individualism.

This connects to Four Thousand Weeks. I agree that mechanizing time made room for productivity to be a topic at all. Once you can measure how long something takes, you can show objectively whether it's "efficient" — and the pressure to be efficient follows.

entries.title: Cognitive Load Theory and its Applications for Learning
entries.creator: Scott H. Young
entries.summary: Notes in Cognitive Load and Worked Example Effect.
entries.search:
Notes in Cognitive Load and Worked Example Effect.

The idea at the center is simple enough to be easy to ignore: working memory is tiny, and the way material is presented decides how much of it is left over for actual learning. Everything practical follows — the Split Attention Effect when text and diagram live apart, the Worked Example Effect when novices study solutions before attempting problems, and the Expertise Reversal Effect when the same help becomes clutter for someone who already knows the material.

The upshot is unglamorous. Cut what's extraneous, sequence from worked examples to independent problems, and stop mistaking struggle for depth when most of the struggle is with the layout. It's also a quiet argument against learning from a browser full of tabs; see The Shallows.

entries.title: Cognitive Load
entries.summary: The amount of information flowing into working memory at any moment. Working memory is the brain's scratchpad: we're only aware of what's in it, and to think about something we've learned, it has to come back up from long-term memory.
entries.search:
The amount of information flowing into working memory at any moment. Working memory is the brain's scratchpad: we're only aware of what's in it, and to think about something we've learned, it has to come back up from long-term memory.

Three kinds, all drawing on the same limited reservoir:

- Intrinsic — effort that belongs to the topic itself.
- Extraneous — effort caused by how the material or task is presented.
- Germane — the work of building a permanent store of knowledge, a schema.

Extraneous load takes room away from intrinsic load. And when working memory is full, germane load — the actual learning — doesn't happen as readily. The schemas we build come out shallower.

The two biggest sources of overload, per The Shallows: problem-solving and divided attention. Which bodes poorly for the web, where the brain regions for both are highly active.

Effects that fall out of it: Split Attention Effect, Worked Example Effect, Expertise Reversal Effect, Completion-Problem Effect, Modality Effect, Seductive Details Theory, Effects of Hyperlinks on Learning.

Also from Cognitive Load Theory and its Applications for Learning, a Scott H. Young podcast.

entries.title: Completion-problem effect
entries.summary: Why it came up: the Worked Example Effect raised worries about passive learning, and learners tended to study worked examples only when they struggled with conventional problems.
entries.search:
Why it came up: the Worked Example Effect raised worries about passive learning, and learners tended to study worked examples only when they struggled with conventional problems.

The fix was paired alternation — study an example, then solve a problem — which recruits both passive and active learning. A completion problem goes further: a partially worked example where the learner completes the key steps.

Result: people learning programming wrote better new programs when their learning was built on completion problems rather than writing programs from scratch.

entries.title: Effects of hyperlinks on learning
entries.summary: Book readers show activity in regions for language, memory, and visual processing. Net users show extensive activity in regions for decision-making and problem-solving — because every link is a decision: click or don't.
entries.search:
Book readers show activity in regions for language, memory, and visual processing. Net users show extensive activity in regions for decision-making and problem-solving — because every link is a decision: click or don't.

Those decisions take up room in working memory, a cognitive tax on moving information into the richer schemas of long-term memory. See Cognitive Load.

- Long-form readers go line by line; web readers scan in an "F" pattern. Only about 18% of an article's information gets read.
- Asked to compare two contrasting texts, people who read them linearly did better than people who switched back and forth.

entries.title: Expertise reversal effect
entries.summary: Instruction that helps learners build long-term schemas works best for novices, who have no such structures to lean on. For experts, less guidance often beats well-guided instruction.
entries.search:
Instruction that helps learners build long-term schemas works best for novices, who have no such structures to lean on. For experts, less guidance often beats well-guided instruction.

Same reason the Worked Example Effect fades with prior knowledge: once a problem-solving schema exists, giving it again is redundant.

The awkward implication is that there's no single best way to teach something; the best way depends on who's in the room. Guidance that holds a novice's hand is, for an expert, just extra material to read and reconcile with what they already know — extraneous load by another name, the same cost as the Split Attention Effect.

The fix is fading: start with full worked solutions, move to partly finished ones (Completion-Problem Effect), then let go entirely. It's also a decent case for skipping the introductory chapters of anything already familiar, and for suspicion of any teaching that never changes as the learner does (Cognitive Load).

entries.title: Technological determinists vs instrumentalists
entries.summary:
- Determinists: the technologies we use change how we think, and we have little to no control over how.
- Instrumentalists: we control technology; it is entirely subservient to the wishes of its user.
entries.search:
- Determinists: the technologies we use change how we think, and we have little to no control over how.
- Instrumentalists: we control technology; it is entirely subservient to the wishes of its user.
 

The Shallows sides with the determinists — the medium, not the content, changes our patterns of perception. Time-Keeping is the example. Technology creates another way of interacting with the world and offloading some previously necessary capabilities to open a new avenue of discovery and innovation. Socrates and Plato once held fears of writing as removing the didactic memory of old, where orators could deliver novels of prose and mythology by memory and the process of dialogue with others were how great ideas were formed.

entries.title: Worked example effect
entries.summary: Novices do better on transfer tasks — using skills in unfamiliar situations — when taught with worked examples than with problem-solving.
entries.search:
Novices do better on transfer tasks — using skills in unfamiliar situations — when taught with worked examples than with problem-solving.

One reason: less extraneous load. Solving a problem from scratch means figuring out how to solve it before you can learn the schema worth storing.

I find this interesting next to The Shallows, where people who learned a game with minimal instruction learned it more robustly than people guided by software. Could the long-term robustness of learning differ between the two groups here too?

And per the Scott H. Young podcast I referenced in Cognitive Load, people with more prior knowledge benefit less — the material is redundant. With a problem-solving schema already in long-term memory, they can segment the problem efficiently and spend working memory on solving it. See Expertise Reversal Effect.

entries.title: Monkey brain mapping experiment
entries.summary: Michael Merzenich used microelectrodes to make fine maps of where a monkey's hand is represented in the brain — which neuron fires when which spot on the hand is touched.
entries.search:
Michael Merzenich used microelectrodes to make fine maps of where a monkey's hand is represented in the brain — which neuron fires when which spot on the hand is touched.

Then he cut the sensory nerve and let it heal. The nerves grew back haphazardly, so touches mapped to the wrong places in the somatosensory cortex. After a few months, the brain had rewoven the map to match the hand again.

Later work confirmed this kind of remapping beyond the somatosensory cortex. The brain is plastic — and, per The Shallows, that plasticity cuts both ways.

entries.title: Self-talk ritual
entries.summary: From Mark Queppet's The Reboot Regimen. The point: improve the quality of internal discussion so the rational mind can interpret emotional responses and steer them toward actions that help.
entries.search:
From Mark Queppet's The Reboot Regimen. The point: improve the quality of internal discussion so the rational mind can interpret emotional responses and steer them toward actions that help.

1. Ground. Tension in the body tracks negative emotion and short-circuits relaxed, rational thinking. A few deep breaths, a body scan, engage the senses.
2. Connect. Bring awareness to the emotional center and observe whatever's there, without judgment. You can't change what's there, only notice it.
3. Translate. Put the felt sense into a sentence. Don't filter — we think a lot of nonsense; we aren't meant to take every thought seriously.
4. Respond — with truth, as a friend, as a leader. Accept the desire, then state honestly what acting on it leads to, and whether it moves you toward your best life.

You have to feed these truths to yourself in the moment.

entries.title: Biphasic sleep and napping
entries.summary: Biphasic sleep is our natural physiological state — before artificial light, humans tended toward two sleeps — and naps can be used to improve performance through the day.
entries.search:
Biphasic sleep is our natural physiological state — before artificial light, humans tended toward two sleeps — and naps can be used to improve performance through the day.

What gets in the way:
- Self-medicating sleepiness with caffeine. Could time the caffeine right before a midday nap instead.
- A workaholic culture that looks down on napping. Worth checking, with Cognitive Journaling, whether I hold beliefs that keep me from using naps.

What the evidence says:
- 10–15 minute naps improve cognitive performance. In some studies 20-minute naps improved reaction time and vigilance without changing subjective sleepiness; 30-minute naps improved both.
- A nap beat 200 mg of caffeine and lasted longer; nap plus caffeine beat either alone. Bright light and face-washing did worse than both.
- Sleep stage matters: stage 4 left people sleepier, REM less sleepy; stage 1 without stage 2 improved alertness.
- In a 4-day visual task, performance fell each session. A 30-minute nap after session two stopped the decline; a 1-hour nap reversed it.
- A Greek study: napping 30 minutes at least 3 times a week went with 37% less risk of dying from a heart attack (64% among working men).

The "perfect" nap is 90 minutes between 1 and 3 pm — its ratio of sleep stages mirrors a night's.

entries.title: Present orientation
entries.summary: Being in the present avoids the short-circuiting of self-conscious thought. Self-conscious thoughts turn into rumination, and attention gets fed into them, taking resources from problem-solving. Like thinking about whether you'll make the s
entries.search:
Being in the present avoids the short-circuiting of self-conscious thought. Self-conscious thoughts turn into rumination, and attention gets fed into them, taking resources from problem-solving. Like thinking about whether you'll make the shot while you're shooting — it takes you out of flow.

That's why spontaneous speaking is hard: the self-conscious circuits switch on.

Ways to cultivate it:
- Reframe challenging questions as the biggest opportunities. Someone challenging you is engaged — they want to understand.
- Shoot for average, fail cheerfully.
- Be obvious; that's where your truest voice is.
- Be uncomfortable enough to plug in — get lost on purpose and see what you find.
